items.title: Here’s who dominated No Surprises Act disputes in 2025 - Modern Healthcare
items.reason: The article analyzes No Surprises Act dispute outcomes and performance data in 2025, which directly relates to IDR process implementation and enforcement effectiveness—key components of NSA revenue-cycle impact.
items.summary: Modern Healthcare reports on which entities dominated No Surprises Act disputes during 2025, analyzing performance patterns in the Independent Dispute Resolution process. The article provides data on dispute outcomes and identifies leading parties in NSA-related litigation and resolution activities. This information is material for revenue-cycle teams assessing compliance strategies, negotiation leverage in balance-billing disputes, and performance benchmarking against industry participants in the IDR system.

items.title: No Surprises Act Enters a New Phase: What Employers and Group Health Plans Need to Know About the 2026 IDR Rules - The National Law Review
items.reason: The article directly addresses upcoming changes to the No Surprises Act's Independent Dispute Resolution (IDR) process for 2026, which is a core component of NSA implementation and rulemaking that affects revenue-cycle operations.
items.summary: The No Surprises Act is entering a new regulatory phase with updated IDR rules taking effect in 2026 that employers and group health plans must understand and implement. The article discusses how the Independent Dispute Resolution process—the mechanism for resolving balance-billing disputes under the NSA—will change in the coming year, affecting how organizations handle surprise billing claims and determinations. Revenue-cycle teams need to prepare for these procedural changes to maintain compliance with federal balance-billing protections and avoid penalties for non-compliance with the updated IDR framework.

items.title: No Surprises Act umpires need complete case files: NAIRO - BenefitsPRO
items.reason: The item directly addresses operational issues within the No Surprises Act's Independent Dispute Resolution (IDR) process, specifically case file completeness requirements that affect how IDR umpires adjudicate disputes.
items.summary: The National Association of Independent Review Organizations (NAIRO) has raised concerns about the need for complete case files in No Surprises Act Independent Dispute Resolution (IDR) proceedings. The article discusses requirements for documentation and case file submission to IDR umpires who adjudicate balance-billing disputes under the No Surprises Act. This operational issue affects how healthcare revenue-cycle teams prepare and submit IDR cases, as incomplete files can delay dispute resolution and impact claim payment outcomes in the federal balance-billing framework.

items.title: Costs tied to No Surprises Act's IDR process hit $22B in 2025, study finds
items.reason: The item reports empirical data on IDR process costs under the No Surprises Act, directly affecting revenue-cycle operations and financial planning for healthcare organizations managing dispute resolution expenses.
items.summary: A new analysis found that costs associated with the No Surprises Act's Independent Dispute Resolution (IDR) process reached $22.4 billion by the end of 2025. This substantial expense figure reflects the financial burden of administering the federal balance-billing protections mandated under the No Surprises Act. Healthcare organizations and revenue-cycle teams managing claim disputes and IDR submissions are directly affected by these escalating operational costs. The data is significant for revenue-cycle planning, as it quantifies the economic impact of IDR compliance and dispute resolution administration on the healthcare system.

items.title: Jefferson and CHOP join antitrust lawsuit over alleged payment suppression - The Business Journals
items.reason: This reports provider litigation against payers alleging payment suppression, which directly falls under payer enforcement and litigation activity that impacts revenue cycle management and reimbursement rates.
items.summary: Jefferson Health and Children's Hospital of Philadelphia (CHOP) have joined an antitrust lawsuit alleging payment suppression by health insurers/payers. The lawsuit challenges payer practices that allegedly suppress provider reimbursement rates below fair market value. This litigation is relevant to revenue-cycle teams because adverse payer payment practices and resulting legal action directly impact provider reimbursement, contract negotiations, and cash flow. The outcome could establish precedent or force payers to adjust payment methodologies affecting provider revenue.

items.title: DOJ settles lawsuit with Medicare Advantage homecare company for $2M - Health Exec
items.reason: This is a DOJ enforcement action and settlement against a Medicare Advantage company, which constitutes regulatory enforcement involving a payer entity and directly impacts revenue-cycle operations.
items.summary: The U.S. Department of Justice settled a lawsuit with a Medicare Advantage homecare company for $2 million. The settlement represents a federal enforcement action against a payer/plan entity, likely involving compliance violations in claims processing, billing, or benefit administration. This type of enforcement action signals potential regulatory scrutiny of MA plan practices and may affect how payers handle homecare claims and reimbursement, impacting provider revenue-cycle operations and payment terms. Revenue-cycle teams should monitor the settlement terms for any broader implications on MA billing standards and compliance requirements.
